newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.S. wants U.N. council to condemn Iraqi flight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants U.N. council to condemn Iraqi flight.

text.p: The United States is pressing for a strong Security Council statement condemning Iraq for violating sanctions by flying pilgrims from Baghdad to Saudi Arabia aboard an Iraqi aircraft, American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson said on Wednesday.
An air embargo is part of the stiff U.N. economic sanctions imposed on Iraq shortly after its August 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

"We are seeking a (Security Council) presidential statement condemning this act, saying this is unacceptable, and asking for a very strong presidential statement," Richardson told reporters after raising the issue during closed-door council consultations on a number of matters.

"It's an outright violation of sanctions. What we have here is once again Iraq defying the international community and defying the U.N. Security Council. We hope and expect the Security Council to take a strong presidential statement as soon as possible," Richardson added.

Iraqi U.N. envoy Nizar Hamdoon, who was called in later by council president Antonio Monteiro of Portugal, told reporters: "I explained to him our position...that this is a purely humanitarian and religious flight, and that we hope that the council takes into consideration not only the feelings of the Iraqi people but also the feelings of the Moslems across the world."

Hamdoon maintained there was "nothing in the Security Council resolutions that prohibit Iraq from flying its airlines, especially if it is not for commercial reasons that could incur financial transactions."
"The Saudi authorities were receptive to the people who arrived there and they processed the passengers and the flight was not interrupted by them," he added.

He said he did not know whether the aircraft in question, which had flown back to Baghdad, would return to Jeddah to fly the pilgrims home. But he added: "Obviously, if you take somebody by plane, you have to return them by plane."

Reports from the region said an Iraqi plane carrying 104 Moslems pilgrims bound for Mecca landed at Jeddah airport after being accompanied by two Saudi Arabian air force jets from the time it entered Saudi airspace from Jordan.
Saudi Interior Minister Prince Nayef said the Iraqi airliner was allowed to enter the kingdom after authorities were told it carried Iraqi pilgrims.

The Security Council issued a statement last Friday criticising Libya for flying pilgrims to Saudi Arabia aboard a Libyan aircraft on March 29 in defiance of U.N. sanctions connected with the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland.

It was the third year in a row that Libya had violated sanctions by flying pilgrims to Jeddah on an unauthorised flight even though the council gave permission for an Egyptian airline to ferry Libyans wishing to make the annual pilgrimage.
In a letter to the council president circulated on Wednesday, Libyan U.N. envoy Abuzed Dorda said the pilgrimage to Mecca was a religious duty for all Moslems and did not require authorisation.

"Its performance and the choice of a means of reaching the Holy Places is one of the rights of a Moslem on which there are no religious restrictions and with respect to which he does not require anyone's intercession or permission," Dorda said.
